Prealgebra · Lesson 2.3

The Zero Power

Solve this lesson →All lessons

Powers grow as the exponent climbs, each step up multiplying by the base again. This section goes the other direction and asks what sits one step below the first power, where the exponent is 00. We will work out what a0a0 equals and why every base gives the same value.

Problem
A lab grows a crystal that triples in width every day. Today the crystal measures 3434 units across. Reading the days backward instead of forward, yesterday it was 3333, the day before 3232, and so on, each earlier day being the next one divided by 33. Keep walking backward one day at a time past 3131. What single number does the crystal measure on the day written 3030?
Show a hint
  • Each step backward in time divides the size by 33. Write the chain 34=81, 33=27, 32=9, 31=334=81, 33=27, 32=9, 31=3 and take one more step.
  • The step from 3131 down to 3030 divides by 33 like every step before it. What is 3÷33÷3?
Show the full solution
Each day backward divides the size by 33, so read the chain downward. 34=81,33=27,32=9,31=334=81,33=27,32=9,31=3 The next step down, from 3131 to 3030, divides by 33 just like all the others. 31÷3=3÷3=131÷3=3÷3=1​ The exponent dropped from 11 to 00, and the size landed on 11.
Problem
Run the same backward walk on a different base to be sure it is not a fluke about 33. A deep-sea probe doubles its stored charge every hour and holds 2525 units right now. Step back hour by hour, each step halving, through 24,23,22,2124,23,22,21, and take one final step. What number does 2020 come out to?
Show a hint
  • Halving 21=221=2 is the last step you need.
  • Every step back divides by the base 22, and the step from 2121 to 2020 is no exception.
Show the full solution
Each hour backward halves the charge, so walk the chain down. 25=32,24=16,23=8,22=4,21=225=32,24=16,23=8,22=4,21=2 One more halving carries 2121 down to 2020. 21÷2=2÷2=121÷2=2÷2=1​ A different base, the same landing. Stepping down past the first power always divides the base by itself and arrives at 11.
Key idea
Any nonzero base raised to the zero power equals 11. a0=1(a≠0)a0=1(a=0) List the powers in decreasing order. Each drop of 11 in the exponent divides the value by aa. Going from a1=aa1=a down to a0a0 divides aa by itself, which is 11.

The staircase is one route to a0a0. Here is a second one, coming straight from the rule for dividing powers with a common base. Both routes reach the same value.

Problem
A relay station sends out 7575 signal pulses and an identical station receives exactly 7575 of them, none lost. The fraction kept is 75757575​. Read it two ways. First, any nonzero quantity divided by itself is some plain number, so what is that number? Second, the quotient rule subtracts the exponents, so what power of 77 does the fraction become? Give the plain number that both readings must agree on.
Show a hint
  • Anything nonzero over itself, like 19191919​ or 75757575​, is a single familiar value.
  • The quotient rule turns 75757575​ into 75−5=7075−5=70. The two readings name the same quantity, so set them equal.
Show the full solution
Read the fraction the everyday way first. Any nonzero amount divided by itself is 11, so 7575=17575​=1. Now read it through the quotient rule, which subtracts exponents on a common base. 7575=75−5=707575​=75−5=70 Both readings describe the exact same fraction, so they must be equal. 70=170=1​ The law forces the same answer the staircase already showed.
Problem
Now mix the zero power into ordinary arithmetic so the order of operations gets a say. A jukebox charges 9090 tokens for a song and 2323 tokens for a movie clip. A student buys five songs and one clip. Evaluate the total 5×90+235×90+23.
Show a hint
  • Powers come before multiplication and addition. Turn 9090 and 2323 into plain numbers first.
  • After replacing the powers, the expression is 5×1+85×1+8.
Show the full solution
Evaluate the powers before anything else. The zero power gives 90=190=1, and 23=823=8. 5×90+23=5×1+85×90+23=5×1+8 Multiplication next, then the addition. 5+8=135+8=13​ A zero power is worth exactly 11 wherever it appears, and order of operations treats it like any other power.
Key idea
The quotient rule gives the zero power directly. For any nonzero aa, anan=an−n=a0,anan​=an−n=a0, and that same fraction is a quantity divided by itself, which is 11. So a0=1a0=1 is the only value that keeps the quotient rule working.

Here is where most slip-ups happen. A zero power equals 11, but you have to check what the exponent is attached to. An exponent applies only to the base directly beneath it, unless parentheses put more underneath. The next two problems look almost identical and come out completely different.

Problem
A perfume maker scales a fragrance note by the amount 6m06m0, where mm is some nonzero number of drops. A rival scales the same note by (6m)0(6m)0. Evaluate both. Enter the value of 6m06m0.
Show a hint
  • In 6m06m0 the exponent sits directly on mm, so it grips mm alone, not the 66 in front.
  • 6m06m0 means 6×(m0)=6×16×(m0)=6×1. The 66 is just sitting there, untouched by the exponent.
Show the full solution
In 6m06m0 the exponent is written directly above mm, so it grips only mm. The 66 is a separate factor multiplied in afterward. 6m0=6×(m0)=6×1=66m0=6×(m0)=6×1=6​ For contrast, (6m)0(6m)0 wraps the whole product inside the parentheses, so the exponent grips all of 6m6m and (6m)0=1(6m)0=1. Same symbols, but the parentheses move the answer from 66 all the way to 11.
Problem
Same idea, a little trickier. A scoreboard shows the quantity −40−40 on one panel and (−4)0(−4)0 on the next. They differ only by a pair of parentheses. Evaluate the first one, −40−40.
Show a hint
  • The exponent grips only the 44. The minus sign is applied last, after the power, the same way −42−42 meant −(42)−(42).
  • −40−40 means −(40)=−(1)−(40)=−(1). The parentheses in (−4)0(−4)0 would change which base the exponent holds.
Show the full solution
The exponent in −40−40 grips only the 44, and the minus sign waits until after the power is done, exactly as −42−42 meant −(42)−(42). −40=−(40)=−(1)=−1−40=−(40)=−(1)=−1​ With the parentheses it flips. (−4)0(−4)0 lets the exponent grip the whole −4−4, and any nonzero base to the zero power is 11, so (−4)0=1(−4)0=1. One little pair of parentheses, opposite signs.
Key idea
An exponent applies only to the base it is attached to, unless parentheses enclose more. So c b0=c×1=ccb0=c×1=c, since the 00 applies to bb alone, not the coefficient cc. But (cb)0=1(cb)0=1, because the parentheses make the whole product the base. Likewise −a0=−(a0)=−1−a0=−(a0)=−1 but (−a)0=1(−a)0=1. Check what the exponent applies to before replacing it with 11.
Fun fact
Pocket calculators did not always agree on 0000, and even today most math leaves it undefined, since the descending-divide story would force a divide by zero. But almost everywhere else a0=1a0=1 is treated as rock solid, and it has a simple reason. An empty product, a multiplication with no factors at all, is defined to be 11, the same way an empty sum is 00. A power a0a0 asks for zero copies of aa multiplied together, which is exactly an empty product. So a0a0 being 11 is the multiplication world starting from its natural blank slate. 🚀

So far the zero has been written in plain sight. It gets more interesting when the exponent is a little expression that happens to work out to zero. The power still collapses to 11, but you have to do the exponent arithmetic first to notice.

Problem
A timer raises base 55 to an exponent built from two settings, computing 5 8−858−8. Evaluate it. Then say what the value would become if the second 88 were changed to a 33, giving 5 8−358−3, so you can feel how fragile the collapse to 11 really is. Enter the value of 5 8−858−8.
Show a hint
  • Always finish the exponent's own arithmetic before touching the base. What is 8−88−8?
  • 5 8−8=5058−8=50, and a nonzero base to the zero power is one specific value.
Show the full solution
Settle the exponent first. Here 8−8=08−8=0, so 5 8−8=50=1.58−8=50=1​. Change that second 88 to a 33 and you get 5 8−3=55=312558−3=55=3125. The collapse to 11 only happens when the exponent arithmetic actually lands on zero.
Problem
A puzzle box opens only if a stored power equals 11. The power is 12 k−k12k−k for whatever nonzero number kk the user dials in. One person dials k=37k=37, another dials k=200k=200, a third dials k=1k=1. For how many of these three dial settings does the box open?
Show a hint
  • Work out the exponent k−kk−k before worrying about the base 1212.
  • k−k=0k−k=0 for every kk, so 12 k−k=12012k−k=120 no matter what was dialed.
Show the full solution
The exponent is k−kk−k, which is 00 for every value of kk, no matter how large or small. 12 k−k=120=112k−k=120=1 So the stored power is 11 for k=37k=37, for k=200k=200, and for k=1k=1 alike. The box opens on all 33​ settings. The base 1212 never mattered, only that the exponent collapsed to zero.
Key idea
Sometimes the zero is not written directly. The exponent is a small expression that works out to 00. Finish the arithmetic in the exponent first, and once it reaches 00 the power equals 11, whatever the base. So 5 8−8=50=158−8=50=1 and a k−k=1ak−k=1 for every kk. Rewriting to a common base often turns up a zero exponent, as when 84212=212212=20=121284​=212212​=20=1.

Two problems left, and they pull the section together. Between them you will find a zero exponent that appears only after you force a common base, an exponent you have to compute first, and an exponent that applies to only part of a product. Order of operations decides each step.

Problem
Rewriting to a common base can hide a zero exponent until you dig it out. Simplify 163212212163​ to a single power of 22, then give its value as a plain number.
Show a hint
  • Write 1616 as a power of 22 so the whole fraction lives on one base.
  • 163=(24)3=212163=(24)3=212. Now divide by subtracting exponents and watch where the exponent lands.
Show the full solution
Put everything on base 22. Since 16=2416=24, the power rule gives 163=(24)3=212163=(24)3=212. Now the fraction shares one base, so subtract exponents. 163212=212212=212−12=20=1212163​=212212​=212−12=20=1​ Once everything was on one base, the exponent collapsed to zero, and the value is 11. Of course 212212212212​ had to be 11 anyway, a thing over itself.
Problem
Evaluate 10−3 w 5−5+(4w)010−3w5−5+(4w)0 for any nonzero ww. The expression is built so the value never depends on ww at all. Find that single value.
Show a hint
  • Two zero powers are hiding here. One has an exponent that computes to zero, w 5−5w5−5. The other wraps a whole product, (4w)0(4w)0.
  • w 5−5=w0=1w5−5=w0=1 but it is multiplied by 33, so that term is 3×1=33×1=3. And (4w)0=1(4w)0=1 on its own. Now it is plain arithmetic.
Show the full solution
The exponent 5−5=05−5=0 sits on ww alone, so w 5−5=w0=1w5−5=w0=1 and 3 w 5−5=33w5−5=3. In (4w)0(4w)0 the parentheses hand the whole product to the exponent, so (4w)0=1(4w)0=1. Working left to right, 10−3+1=8.10−3+1=8​. Both zero powers collapse to 11 whatever ww is, which is why ww never reaches the answer.

Practice these ideas

Practice
You already ride the exponent laws up and down. This set walks one specific rung, the strange step where the exponent lands on zero, and asks what a base raised to nothing could possibly equal. Two different roads lead to the same place.
Practice
A tide chart counts grains of light on a sensor. At three flashes the reading is 63=21663=216, at two flashes 62=3662=36, at one flash 61=661=6. Each step down the chart divides the reading by 66. Take one more step down, to zero flashes, and read off 6060.
Show the solution
Each rung down the chart divides by the base. The reading at one flash is 66, so the step down to zero flashes is 60=6÷6=1.60=6÷6=1​. This is not guesswork. Once each step is a division by 66, the rung below 6161 has to be 11.
Practice
A relay station sends 4949 pulses east and the same 4949 pulses west, then asks how many times as many went east as west. That is the quotient 49494949​. Find it two ways, once by the quotient rule that subtracts the exponents, and once by remembering what any number over itself must be. What single value do both give?
Show the solution
By the quotient rule, 4949=49−9=40.4949​=49−9=40. But the same fraction is just one quantity over an identical copy of itself, which is always 11. The two readings have to agree, so 40=1.40=1​. Equal pulses east and west, so of course the ratio is one, and that pins down what 4040 means.
Practice
For any nonzero base aa, a0=1.a0=1. Two roads arrive here. Stepping down a ladder of powers divides by aa each time, so the rung below a1a1 is a÷a=1a÷a=1. And the quotient rule turns anananan​ into an−n=a0an−n=a0, which is also 11 because anything nonzero over itself is 11. The zero power is exactly the value that keeps the exponent laws running with no exceptions.
Practice
A vault timer raises 33 to an exponent it computes on the spot, and today that exponent is 7−77−7. The whole reading is therefore 3 7−737−7. What number does the vault display?
Show the solution
Finish the exponent first. Since 7−7=07−7=0, the reading is 3 7−7=30=1.37−7=30=1​. Whenever the exponent collapses to zero, the whole power flattens to 11, no matter how large the base looks.
Practice
A trivia host stacks three different scores, 5050 for the first team, 120120 for the second, and 10001000 for the third, then adds them. A player groans that the third team must dwarf the others. Find the sum and explain why the sizes of the bases never mattered.
Show the solution
A zero power erases the base entirely. Every nonzero base to the zero power is 11, so 50=150=1, 120=1120=1, and 1000=11000=1. Adding the three equal terms, 1+1+1=3.1+1+1=3​. The 100100 carried no extra weight. Under a zero exponent the base stops mattering, and only how many terms you have decides the total.
Practice
A florist labels two boxes. The first reads 14×t014×t0 and the second reads (14t)0(14t)0, where tt is some nonzero number of tulips. The florist swears the two labels are different numbers. Work out the value of each label, then give the sum of the two values.
Show the solution
The labels are 1414 and 11, so the sum is 14+1=15.14+1=15​. In 14×t014×t0 the exponent sits on tt alone, so t0=1t0=1 and that label is 14×1=1414×1=14. In (14t)0(14t)0 the parentheses gather the whole product 14t14t under the zero, and any nonzero amount to the zero power is 11. The florist is right, since the labels really do differ. Watch the parentheses and you know what the zero power covers.
Practice
An exponent grips only the base written directly beneath it, unless parentheses gather more under it. So c×x0=cc×x0=c, because the zero touches xx alone and leaves the coefficient cc standing. But (cx)0=1(cx)0=1, because the parentheses hand the entire product to the zero. Watch the parentheses and you always know what the zero power covers.
Practice
A scoreboard evaluates 100−7×30+24100−7×30+24 by the usual order of operations. What does it show?
Show the solution
Evaluate the powers first. The nonzero base gives 30=130=1, and 24=1624=16, so the line becomes 100−7×1+16100−7×1+16. Multiply next, 7×1=77×1=7, then work left to right. 100−7+16=109100−7+16=109​ The zero power turned into a 11 and slid into the arithmetic like any other number.
Practice
A thermostat shows (−8)0(−8)0 on its left panel and −80−80 on its right panel. With squares those two readings came out opposite, since (−8)2=64(−8)2=64 while −82=−64−82=−64. Find each reading now and then subtract the right panel from the left.
Show the solution
On the left, the parentheses hand the whole −8−8 to the zero, and −8−8 is a nonzero base, so (−8)0=1(−8)0=1. On the right, the exponent touches only the 88, so −80=−(80)=−(1)=−1−80=−(80)=−(1)=−1. Subtracting the right panel from the left, 1−(−1)=2.1−(−1)=2​. Unlike the square case, the sizes match at 11, but the minus on the right flips its sign, so the panels still disagree.
Practice
The zero power is not a special law bolted on from outside. It is forced by the laws you already have. Watch a3×a0a3×a0. The product rule says add exponents, giving a3+0=a3a3+0=a3. So multiplying by a0a0 must leave a3a3 untouched, which means a0a0 can only be the number that changes nothing under multiplication, and that number is 11. The same argument works for any base, which is why mathematicians say a0=1a0=1 is the only choice that keeps the whole system honest. 🚀
Practice
A lab writes a count as 49376×7276493​×72. Every base is really a power of 77. Rewrite to that one base, then evaluate the whole thing.
Show the solution
Send everything to base 77. The power rule gives 493=(72)3=76493=(72)3=76, so 49376×72=7676×72=76−6×72=70×72.76493​×72=7676​×72=76−6×72=70×72. The zero power is 11, and multiplying by 11 changes nothing, so the count is 1×72=491×72=49​. Forcing a single base let the bulky front fraction vanish to 11, leaving one tidy power.
Practice
A receipt shows a total of (24×54)×90(24×54)×90 cents. Write the total as an ordinary number and count how many digits it has.
Show the solution
The factor 9090 is 11, so it drops away and leaves 24×5424×54. A 22 and a 55 make a 1010, and four such pairs give 24×54=(2×5)4=104=10000.24×54=(2×5)4=104=10000. That is a 11 trailed by four zeros, so the total has 55​ digits. The zero power was a harmless 11 hiding in plain sight.
Practice
Three habits carry the zero power. When an exponent works out to zero, the whole power flattens to 11 before anything else happens. When a power meets an identical copy in a quotient, the quotient rule sends it to a zero power, which is 11. And a stray a0a0 factor is just 11 under multiplication, so it can be erased without changing a thing. Rewriting to a common base is what makes those identical copies appear.
Practice
Collapse this tower to one number. 85×20215×2321585×20​×23 Send every base to 22, and watch for the place where a power divided by its twin disappears.
Show the solution
Push everything to base 22. The factor 20=120=1 drops out, and 85=(23)5=21585=(23)5=215, so the front becomes 215215=215−15=20=1215215​=215−15=20=1. That leaves 1×23=8.1×23=8​. Once every base was a 22, the whole fraction folded down to 11 and only 2323 was left.
Practice
A puzzle box first simplifies the inside of (3632×34)25(32×3436​)25, then raises that result to the 2525th power. Find the number the box prints.
Show the solution
Work the inside before the outer exponent. The product rule gathers the denominator into 32×34=3632×34=36, so the inside is 3636=36−6=30=1.3636​=36−6=30=1. Raising that to the 2525th power, the base is now 11, and 11 multiplied by itself any number of times is still 11. 125=1125=1​ The outer exponent is large, but once the inside collapsed to 11 the height of the tower stopped mattering.
Practice
Evaluate this whole expression, watching every parenthesis. (−3)0+(−3)2−30×32(−3)0+(−3)2−30×32 A classmate guesses it is some large number. Find the exact value.
Show the solution
Read each piece by what its exponent grips. The whole −3−3 is a nonzero base, so (−3)0=1(−3)0=1. An even power of a negative is positive, so (−3)2=9(−3)2=9. And 30=130=1. The expression becomes 1+9−30×32=1+9−1×9.1+9−30×32=1+9−1×9. Order of operations multiplies before subtracting, so 1×9=91×9=9, leaving 1+9−9=1.1+9−9=1​. Two different zero powers, two different jobs, and the whole thing settles on a single 11.
